opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the limits right now are less about raw intelligence and more about reliability over long horizons.

If you give a strong model a single, well-scoped task, like "write this function" or "summarize this document," it's often already better than most people. But an agent isn't doing one step. It's doing fifty or a hundred steps in a row, and every step has some small chance of going wrong. Those errors compound. A 95% success rate per step sounds great, but chain enough of them together and the whole task falls apart. So the real bottleneck is whether the agent can notice it has drifted, recover, and keep the goal in mind over a long time.

The second limit is context, and I don't just mean context-window length. Humans doing real work carry a huge amount of implicit knowledge: why this codebase is structured this way, what my manager actually cares about, which customer is sensitive about what. Agents usually start each task almost from zero. Memory and accumulated understanding of a specific environment are still very primitive, and that's a big part of why agents feel like a brilliant intern on their first day, every day.

Third is the environment itself. Most of our software, websites, and internal tools were designed for humans clicking around, not for agents. A lot of failures aren't the model being dumb. They come from messy interfaces, missing permissions, ambiguous state, things that break silently. Part of the progress will come from the world becoming more agent-friendly, not just from models getting smarter.

The last one, which people underestimate, is judgment about when to stop and ask. A good human colleague knows when something is outside their authority, or when an action is irreversible and they should check first. Agents are still uneven at that calibration. Sometimes they're too timid and ask about everything. Sometimes they're too confident and do something you really didn't want. Getting that balance right is as much a trust problem as a capability problem.

So my mental model is that intelligence is no longer the scarcest thing. Reliability, memory, good environments, and calibrated judgment are where the frontier is now. When those improve, I think we'll see a fairly sudden jump: from agents as impressive demos to agents you actually hand real work to and walk away from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that the limits we see today are less about intelligence and more about reliability and context.

If you give an agent a well-defined task that takes five minutes, it does remarkably well. If you give it something that takes five hours, with many dependent steps, the failure modes change. A small misjudgment early on compounds. The agent doesn't always notice it has drifted off course, and it rarely knows when to stop and ask. Humans have an intuition for "something feels wrong here," and that sense is still quite weak in agents.

The second limit is context. An agent only knows what's in front of it. A new employee learns a company's unwritten rules over months: who to ask, what not to touch, what "done" actually means on this team. An agent starts almost from zero every time, and the tooling for carrying that knowledge forward is still immature. Memory systems exist, but they are brittle.

The third is verification. Agents are now good at producing plausible work, and plausible is dangerous. Code that compiles but is subtly wrong, a summary that reads smoothly but misstates a key number. The gap between "looks right" and "is right" is where most of the real risk sits, and closing it requires the agent to check its own output as rigorously as a skeptical reviewer would.

So I would say the frontier isn't raw capability anymore. It is judgment over long horizons, accumulated context, and the discipline to verify before declaring success. Those are the things that separate a demo from something you'd trust with real work.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest limit is the gap between doing a task once and doing it reliably. An agent can give a very impressive demonstration, but if you ask it to handle a slightly different situation, recover from an error, or work toward a goal over many steps, its weaknesses become much more visible. Small mistakes accumulate, and it may not recognize when it has gone off track.

There’s also a difference between following an instruction and understanding what someone actually wants. In real work, goals are often vague, constraints are unstated, and priorities change. A useful agent needs to know when it can make a reasonable judgment and when it should ask a question.

So I’d look less at whether an agent can complete a particular task and more at how much supervision it needs. Can it check its work? Can it recognize uncertainty? Can it recover safely? For me, those are the things that determine how much responsibility we can actually give it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limit is the gap between doing something impressive once and doing it reliably over time. An agent can produce a convincing plan, use tools, and complete several steps, but as the task gets longer, small mistakes can accumulate. It may misunderstand the goal, miss a constraint, or fail to notice that an earlier action didn’t work.

There’s also a difference between having access to information and having enough context to make a good decision. In real work, people rely on unstated priorities, relationships, and experience. An agent often sees only a small part of that picture.

So I’d judge an agent less by how autonomous it looks and more by whether it knows when to act, when to verify, and when to ask for help. Today, agents are most useful when the task has clear boundaries and the results can be checked. Greater autonomy becomes valuable as that reliability improves.
